use(store) benchmarks at a glance

Every use(store) benchmark result on one page. The benchmark report and the Context comparison explain each one.

Measured on React 0.0.0-experimental-a3d8e745-20261101 (a3d8e745), compiler c59ecf06d45b47db, results pinned 2026-11-02.

  • Main suite, matches or beats

    39/42

    configurations, against the faster of Redux and Zustand, with the compiler

  • Main suite, losses

    3

    all of them in selection, when every row reads the selection

  • Selection sweeps, keyed selection wins

    14/14

    configurations won (it isn't timed in the main suite)

  • Derived-data spike, weakMemo wins

    12/12

    configurations that do any work, won against Redux

  • One context, matches or beats

    35/42

    configurations with the compiler, and a context per slice never wins

  • Counted results, losses

    41/224

    across the headline, the granular control, the ported Redux suites, the fairness run against Redux, the sweeps, and the spike (the controls aren't counted)

Explain →

It wins every conditional-read and add / remove configuration

Against the faster of Redux and Zustand, adding or removing a row is 2.9–7.8× faster, and conditional reads are 2.4–4.2× faster. Add / remove mostly measures list reconciliation, because every variant re-renders every row.

Keyed selection wins every selection sweep

Keyed selection wins every selection configuration (14 of 14), and every entity configuration (14 of 14).

Verdicts with the compiler, under the restart rule. role: unread update (no work).

Plain use(store) is 1.1–1.4× slower against the fastest of Redux and Zustand. With weakMemo (store-memo) it's 1.3–1.5× faster.

Explain →

With more readers, plain use(store) falls further behind

store-memo stays ahead of Redux (1.4–1.9× faster), and plain use(store) falls further behind as the readers grow.

What the compiler buys each approach. Bold: faster or tied with it.

The compiler helps one context far more than use(store) on entity edits and the conditional reads, where one context re-renders many more components. It helps a context per slice far more only on entity edits.

Explain →

Without the compiler, one context wins only in subscribe churn

Without the compiler, use(store) against one context is 1.05× slower to 57× faster (24 faster, 15 tie, 3 slower), and against a context per slice it's up to 62× faster (40 faster, 2 tie).

Without the same-element bailout

The bailout helps most on selection, subscribe churn, and add / remove

Without the bailout, use(store) with the compiler matches or beats the faster of Redux and Zustand in 24 of 28 configurations: 1.4× slower to 9.2× faster (22 faster, 2 tie, 4 slower). With it (the head build, same configurations): 26 of 28: 1.1× slower to 9.2× faster (25 faster, 1 tie, 2 slower).

scenariowithout the bailout, vs the faster of Redux and Zustandwhat the bailout buys
Selection0 faster · 1 tie · 3 slowerup to 1.3× faster (3 faster, 1 tie)
Entity edit4 faster · 0 tie · 0 slowerup to 1.1× faster (1 faster, 3 tie)
Filter4 faster · 0 tie · 0 slowerup to 1.1× faster (1 faster, 3 tie)
Conditional read (inline)4 faster · 0 tie · 0 slowerup to 1.1× faster (1 faster, 3 tie)
Conditional read (child component)4 faster · 0 tie · 0 slowerup to 1.04× faster (2 faster, 2 tie)
Subscribe churn2 faster · 1 tie · 1 slower1.1–1.2× faster
Add / remove4 faster · 0 tie · 0 slower1.2× faster

Without the same-element bailout, compiler on. Never part of the headline.

Over the 28 configurations the build without the bailout measured, use(store) with the compiler matches or beats the faster of Redux and Zustand in 26 with the bailout, and in 24 without it.

Explain →

use(store) uses less memory per row than Redux or Zustand

With the compiler at the largest size, use(store) uses 2,901 bytes per row, against 4,549 for Zustand and 7,191 for Redux.

These are synthetic benchmarks, small apps built to isolate one thing each, with no data from a real app yet. How the numbers were measured.
